111.quote_or_event: During the fighting at Anandpur, Bhai Kanhaiya, a Sikh of Guru Gobind Singh, carried water to the wounded of both armies, Sikh and Mughal alike. When Sikhs complained that he was helping the enemy, he answered that he saw no enemy, only the Guru in every face, and the Guru approved and gave him ointment to dress the wounds of all.
111.explanation: The story is the classic Sikh image of service that makes no distinction between friend and foe; it inspired later Sikh humanitarian seva.
111.tie_back: It is a lived version of the Kural's fitness: dealing rightly and equally with enemies, strangers and friends.
111.source: SikhNet, 'The Story of Bhai Kanhaiya Singh' (paraphrase of the Sikh tradition)
111._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on equal treatment of friend and foe; the account is well known in Sikh tradition but the source is a popular Sikh website and details vary between tellings.

112.quote_or_event: “It does not run short, and it does not run out.”
112.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the wealth of the Lord's Name as a treasure that never diminishes however much it is used.
112.tie_back: The Kural promises that the upright person's prosperity does not crumble; Gurbani makes the same claim, but for the spiritual wealth of the righteous rather than material gain.
112.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 375, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
112._accuracy_note: Next-best: shares the image of wealth that never decays, but concerns the Naam, not the material prosperity of the just, and says nothing of descendants.

113.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
113.explanation: Guru Nanak makes taking another's due, haq paraia, as abhorrent as the strongest taboo of each community.
113.tie_back: The Kural tells us to give up at once any gain won by abandoning fairness, however good it looks; Guru Nanak treats such gain as utterly forbidden food.
113.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
113._accuracy_note: Strong fit on renouncing unjust gain; the Kural's 'that very day' urgency and its concession that such gain may look beneficial are not in the verse.

114.quote_or_event: “Celebrated and approved is the coming into the world of such a person, who saves all his generations as well.”
114.explanation: Guru Amar Das says a life is approved when its good extends to the whole family line.
114.tie_back: Read with Parimelazhagar's gloss of echcham as offspring, the Kural says the worth of the just is shown in what they leave behind; Gurbani likewise judges a life by its benefit to the generations.
114.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1094, Raag Maaroo, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
114._accuracy_note: Next-best: shares the idea that a life's worth appears in its effect on descendants, but the saving is spiritual and the verse does not speak of justice or of revealing it.

115.quote_or_event: “That man, who in the midst of pain, does not feel pain, who is not affected by pleasure, affection or fear, and who looks alike upon gold and dust;”
115.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person who stays even and unshaken through loss and gain, pain and pleasure.
115.tie_back: The Kural says loss and gain will surely come and the noble person's ornament is a heart that does not bend in either; Guru Tegh Bahadur paints the same steadiness.
115.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
115._accuracy_note: Strong fit on equanimity in loss and gain; the Kural stresses unswerving fairness, while the verse stresses inner detachment.

116.quote_or_event: “Do not harbor evil intentions against others in your mind, and you shall not be troubled, O Siblings of Destiny, O friends.”
116.explanation: Guru Arjan ties freedom from suffering to keeping ill will toward others out of one's heart.
116.tie_back: The Kural tells the person whose heart turns to wrong to read it as a sign of coming ruin; Gurbani teaches the converse: keep the heart free of ill intent and trouble will not come.
116.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
116._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on wrong intention leading to one's own harm; the Kural's self-diagnosis ('I am heading for ruin') and its focus on partiality are not explicit.

117.quote_or_event: “You are the wealth of the poor, the Guru of the guru-less, the honor of the dishonored.”
117.explanation: Guru Nanak praises God as the honour of those the world holds in no esteem.
117.tie_back: The Kural says the world will not count the poverty of the upright as a fall; Gurbani goes further, saying the poor and dishonoured have God as their wealth and honour.
117.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 992, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
117._accuracy_note: Next-best: affirms dignity in poverty but does not tie it to the poor person's fairness, and speaks of God's regard rather than the world's.

118.quote_or_event: “Mind is the scale, consciousness the weights, and the performance of Your service is the appraiser.”
118.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the merchant's balance as an image for the inner discipline by which a person weighs rightly.
118.tie_back: The Kural's balance-beam first sets itself level and then weighs without leaning; Guru Nanak likewise makes the mind itself the scale that must be true.
118.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 731, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
118._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: shares the balance image and the inner-steadiness idea; the verse is about appraising God's virtues, not impartial judgment between people.

119.quote_or_event: “They alone are true, whose love for God is deep and heart-felt. Those who have one thing in their heart, and something else in their mouth, are judged to be false.”
119.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose verses are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, condemns the gap between heart and mouth.
119.tie_back: The Kural says straight speech counts as fairness only when the heart itself is free of crookedness; Farid says the same split between inner and outer marks a person as false.
119.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
119._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the agreement of inner and outer; the context is sincerity in love of God rather than impartiality, and Farid is a Muslim saint whose bani the Gurus included in Sikh scripture.

120.quote_or_event: Macauliffe records that Nanak, as storekeeper for Governor Daulat Khan at Sultanpur, carried out his duties to everyone's satisfaction, giving most of his own allowance to the poor; when weighing out provisions and reaching thirteen, tera, he would repeat the word, which also means 'Thine'. When complaints of extravagance were investigated, the store was found full and his accounts correct, with money owed to him.
120.explanation: The story presents Guru Nanak's honest handling of another's goods as an act of devotion.
120.tie_back: It matches the Kural's rule for traders: guard other people's goods as carefully as one's own.
120.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, ch. III, pp. 33, 42-43 (paraphrase)
120._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on honest stewardship of another's goods; it is a hagiographic Janamsakhi-based account, and its point is devotion as much as commercial fairness.
